cards.title: Russia, North Korea sign economic protocol; Seoul watches for Kim China visit
cards.summary: North Korea and Russia held their economic committee in Pyongyang on 27 November and agreed new projects; state media did not mention arms. Seoul's spy agency is watching for a possible Kim Jong Un visit to China. Putin commissioned the submarine Perm, which Moscow says is the first armed with Zircon hypersonic missiles.
cards.body:
The week after the Shenzhen summit, the three-way relationship among Moscow, Beijing and Pyongyang showed activity on the economic and symbolic side rather than the military one. North Korea and Russia held the 13th session of their intergovernmental committee in Pyongyang, signed a protocol and confirmed projects in power, agriculture, health and education; Kim met the Russian minister, and North Korean state media used the language of 'alliance'. The report said nothing about weapons. That matters because Ukraine's military intelligence claimed on 26 November that Pyongyang had paused arms deliveries to Russia and closed its airspace to Russian military transports after a row over Moscow's outreach to Seoul. The committee meeting neither confirms nor refutes that claim, and no second government or major news agency has reported a pause, so the board keeps it labelled as a claim.

South Korea's National Intelligence Service said it is watching for a possible Kim visit to China; a diplomatic source told Yonhap it could come at any time, and observers point to early December. A visit soon after Xi hosted Trump and Putin would show Beijing keeping its own channel to Pyongyang while it manages Washington.

On the Russian side, Putin attended the commissioning of the Yasen-M submarine Perm at Severodvinsk on 27 November. Moscow says it is the first boat armed with Zircon hypersonic missiles, and Putin said five more nuclear submarines will join the navy by 2030. Yasen-M boats carry cruise missiles rather than the ballistic missiles of Russia's strategic submarines, and no change in nuclear posture was announced, so the board reads the ceremony as fleet renewal and signalling.

China's own moves stayed economic: its commerce ministry called the US tariff probe unilateral and reserved the right to respond, but announced no countermeasure. The questions for the next fortnight are whether Kim travels to Beijing, whether anyone independent confirms or denies the North Korean pause, and how Beijing answers the tariff proposal before the trade truce expires in January.

cards.confidenceNote: Plea, alert and listing read on Military Times, Breaking Defense, BBC and Al Jazeera pages; the ship-cyber probe rests on a WSJ report carried by gCaptain.
cards.title: US Army sergeant pleads guilty to passing HIMARS secrets to China
cards.summary: Army supply sergeant Jian Zhao pleaded guilty on 24 November to conspiring to pass defence information, including HIMARS material, to China-connected people. Britain warned defence firms of Russian proxy arson the same day. The US blacklisted Megaspeed on 23 November, and the WSJ reports a probe of suspected Iranian cyberattacks on up to 50 ships.
cards.body:
Four cases in three days show the technology contest running on several fronts at once, and each points at a different adversary.

The Zhao plea is the China file. A supply sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord admitted conspiring from late 2021 to early 2025 to sell national defence information, including excerpts of HIMARS technical manuals, photographs of restricted briefings and government computers, to people connected to China; a co-conspirator had already pleaded guilty and sentencing is set for 1 March 2027. HIMARS is the long-range rocket system at the centre of US plans for Taiwan and the Philippines, so the target matters more than the sums involved, which were small.

The Megaspeed listing is the export-control file. On 23 November the Commerce Department added the Singapore data-centre firm at the centre of the Nvidia diversion affair, and six other Southeast Asian firms, to its Entity List; Singapore opened its own investigation. Beijing has not yet answered, and the board will watch whether it uses its own licensing tools on rare earths or drone parts in reply, as it did in October.

The Russia file is sabotage rather than theft. Britain's protective security agency, run by MI5, told defence firms and suppliers to Ukraine on 24 November that Russia has stepped up attempts to sabotage European defence sites, mainly through arson by low-level proxies hired online. It is a warning, not a new incident, but it formalises what Estonia, Germany and Denmark have attributed case by case, and it comes a week after the US charged a Russian with spying on Palantir staff in California.

The Iran file is the least certain. The Wall Street Journal reported on 23 November that US authorities are investigating suspected cyberattacks on as many as 50 tankers and chemical carriers, some sent bomb threats, with Iran the main suspect and Russia a possible one. No US agency has attributed the attacks on the record, and Reuters could not verify the report. If it holds, the Hormuz confrontation has a cyber front against commercial shipping alongside the drones and projectiles UKMTO logs.

What would change the picture: a named US attribution of the ship attacks; a Chinese counter-listing after Megaspeed; or a first sabotage incident in Britain tied to the proxies the alert describes.

cards.title: US disables blockade runner as Kuwait protests Iranian attacks
cards.summary: US aircraft disabled the merchant ship Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on 26 November, at least the 15th ship disabled since April. Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador on 27 November; Italy says the drone that killed two Italians was Iranian-made. The FT reports a drone swarm was repelled at RAF Lakenheath on 13 November.
cards.body:
The blockade is the part of the war that is still being fought every week. On 26 November US aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman and disabled its propulsion, CENTCOM said, after the ship left Bandar Abbas apparently bound for Singapore; the crew was unharmed. By Al Jazeera's count of US statements it is at least the 15th ship disabled since the blockade began in April and the sixth since it resumed in July; CENTCOM says 158 ships have been redirected. The previous one was on 7 November. A day later Iran's navy commander said on state television that Iran would 'break the naval blockade' and drive US forces out of the region's waters, and the Guard said two tankers using an 'unauthorised' route met a mine and a forced turnaround; neither claim has been verified.

The Kuwait deaths moved into diplomacy. Kuwait's foreign ministry summoned Iran's ambassador on 27 November to protest continued Iranian attacks, and Italy's foreign minister said Kuwaiti investigators had found the drone was made in Iran. Iran denies launching it and has offered a joint investigation. Manufacture is not the same as launch point, which is why the board still records the attribution as Kuwait's and Italy's, beside Iran's denial.

The war's reach into allied homelands also came into sharper view. The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that US forces used counter-drone systems to repel about six drones swarming RAF Lakenheath on 13 November and that Iran is suspected; Britain's defence ministry confirmed only an incident that was quickly resolved. The board already carried the incident with its origin unknown; the new elements are the swarm and the suspicion.

The information contest sharpened too. CENTCOM rejected an Iranian commander's claims that Iran had struck USS Abraham Lincoln and retaken two seized tankers, saying the Lincoln group was never hit and went home in October. That leaves the identity of Trump's 'extra carrier' open.

South of the Gulf, armed people seized a cargo ship 64 nautical miles off Balhaf on 28 November, UKMTO said, with no group named, while the Saudi-led coalition kept striking Houthi areas. The tactical questions now are whether Iran attempts anything at sea against the blockade, whether the US answers on Iranian soil, and who took the ship off Yemen.

cards.confidenceNote: US alert via Euronews; Trump remarks via Times of Israel; Iran position via Iran International and The New Arab (analysis); Iran reopening terms on board from 23 Nov.
cards.title: Talks with Iran stall as US tells citizens to leave
cards.summary: Indirect US-Iran contacts are deadlocked, with Iran holding to its conditions for reopening Hormuz. Iran offered on 23 November to reopen the strait within two days if hostilities, the blockade and sanctions end. On 25 November the US told its citizens to leave Iran, and Trump said the war is funded through January.
cards.body:
The diplomatic track has narrowed to two incompatible offers. Iran's foreign ministry said on 23 November that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if hostilities, the blockade and sanctions end, while vowing 'all available means' against the blockade. Washington's position, as Trump set it out to Fox News, is that the preliminary Islamabad understanding was 'a waste of time' and that he will finish the war 'one way or the other'. On 12 November he told the Vice-President to drop the talks.

Contacts have not ended. Kushner says meetings with Tehran officials continue under Vance's oversight and that all options remain on the table, but reporting from the region describes the indirect channel as deadlocked, with Iran not moving on its conditions. Qatar, the main mediator, is under strain: Iran summoned its envoy on 23 November over a joint Qatar-Germany statement, and a Qatari delegation's 20 November visit to Tehran produced no announced result.

Two US statements on 25 November shift the frame from talks to timing. The embassy alert told Americans to leave Iran immediately, warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly and that Iran, the Houthis and aligned groups may target US interests. Trump said the war is funded through the end of January, which sets a horizon without setting a date. Iran's Guard answered with warnings of 'new targets, weapons and offensive plans' if the US or Israel 'make another mistake'.

The board reads this as a stalled track with escalation risk rising, not a broken one: mediators remain engaged and no party has declared talks over. The deal that matters, reopening the strait in exchange for lifting the blockade, has the same shape it had in June; what has changed is that each side now conditions it on the other moving first. An agreement before 30 November looks very unlikely.

cards.confidenceNote: Gaza strikes via France 24 and BBC (on board); Netanyahu trial development read at BBC; joint strike planning is one NYT report.
cards.title: Judges urge dropping Netanyahu charges as Israel hits Hamas leaders
cards.summary: Judges in Netanyahu's corruption trial suggested on 25 November that prosecutors drop the bribery charges. An Israeli strike killed Hamas's internal security chief in Gaza on 24 November. Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form a government, faces a 6 December deadline.
cards.body:
Israel's war in Gaza has become a campaign against Hamas's security leadership under a ceasefire that both sides say the other violates. An Israeli strike killed the head of Hamas's internal security apparatus on 24 November. It follows the 18 November armoured incursion across the ceasefire line, which displaced 5,200 people, and the killing of the Rafah brigade commander on 14 November.

On Iran, the New York Times reported that US and Israeli officials have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on energy targets, and on 25 November Trump said the war is funded through the end of January, a horizon that would bound any renewed joint campaign.

Israel's own politics are in flux. Judges in Netanyahu's corruption trial suggested on 25 November that prosecutors drop the bribery charges, a boost for the caretaker prime minister, who called for the trial to end immediately. Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form a government, faces a 6 December deadline after the Likud-Yashar unity talks collapsed on 22 November.

For the alliance, the question is whether a change of Israeli government changes the Iran calculus. A new coalition would keep the Gaza security campaign but could weigh a second round against Iran differently from Netanyahu, which would leave Washington, not Jerusalem, setting the timetable the funding remark implies.

cards.confidenceNote: Facts read on Al Jazeera, Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Post and The New Arab pages; band judgements are the board's, under its scoring method.
cards.title: US disables a blockade runner and drones fly at Moscow; risk holds
cards.summary: US aircraft disabled a ship running the Iran blockade on 26 November, and a drone attack Kuwait blames on Iran killed two Italians. Ukraine sent hundreds of drones toward Moscow, and a Russian strike killed seven in Nizhyn. The board's four axes hold at 75, 70, 60 and 60, a score of 66.
cards.body:
Both wars produced action this week without crossing a new threshold. In the Gulf, the US used force to enforce its blockade for the first time since 7 November, disabling the Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman, and Iran's navy vowed to break the blockade. A drone attack that Kuwait and Italy blame on Iran killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti air-defence site, the first deaths on a Gulf host state's soil in the November exchange, and Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador. Washington has not struck Iranian territory since 17 November.

In Europe, Ukraine's drones reached the Moscow region in large numbers and its General Staff says it hit a plant making Iskander missile fuel, while Russia's strikes killed seven people in Nizhyn. Kyiv put a Black Sea ceasefire to Moscow, which wants oil shipments included. A Russian convoy to Libya turned back after the Merkury sinking.

The four axes hold. Kinetic stays at 75: firing on a blockade runner is enforcement of a blockade the board already scores, and the Kuwait deaths were scored on 27 November. Great-power stays at 70: there is no direct US-Iran exchange on Iranian soil and no US-Russia contact. WMD stays at 60: the new Russian submarine is a cruise-missile boat, and no change in nuclear posture was announced. Alliance stays at 60: Kuwait's protest is aimed at Iran, the Mecca pact partners are closing ranks around Saudi Arabia, and European friction over the sanctions package and Nord Stream is a dispute among allies, not a break with Washington.

What would move the score: a US strike on Iranian territory or an Iranian attack on a US warship (kinetic and great-power up); a NATO shoot-down or casualty from Russian fire on allied soil; a second deadly strike on a Gulf host state paired with a US response; US tariffs on the EU actually imposed (alliance up); or Russian acceptance of a Black Sea ceasefire, which would argue the other way.

cards.confidenceNote: Rosstat analysis read at Mediazona, NYT, The Moscow Times and Euronews; Poland via Kyiv Independent and France 24; strikes via Kyiv Post, Al Jazeera and The Moscow Times.
cards.title: Leaked Rosstat records show at least 490,000 Russian war dead
cards.summary: Meduza and Mediazona found at least 490,000 Russian military deaths registered by late September in leaked Rosstat data; adding the missing, they estimate more than 700,000. The Kremlin declined comment. Poland will create a no-fly zone on its Ukraine border, and both sides struck energy and cities again.
cards.body:
The war's cost to Russia now has a number taken from Russia's own registry. Hackers from the Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow announced a breach of Rosstat on 1 November and gave the records to journalists from 8 November; Meduza and Mediazona cleaned 11.7 million records covering January 2021 to 29 September 2026 and identified at least 490,000 deaths of Russian servicemen already registered. That figure is a floor. Deaths are registered with delays of months, and missing soldiers often a year or more later; modelling those, the authors estimate the true toll at about 700,000 by September, rising to 720,000 or more by the autumn. Other teams working from the leak reached counts of 472,000 to 537,000, the higher ones including foreign nationals. The Kremlin declined to comment, saying only the defence ministry can give figures; it has not done so since September 2022. The board shows the floor and the estimate as two figures, and compares neither with Ukraine's General Staff tally, which counts killed and wounded.

The spillover track is where the war is changing shape. After Russian cruise missiles fell on Polish soil on 20 November and a drone crossed the Lublin region on 23 November, Poland announced a no-fly zone at least 10 km deep along its Ukraine border, with rules due by early January that let pilots engage without visual identification. Trump and Rutte jointly urged Russia to avoid actions that widen the war. Estonia expelled a Russian worker at a border oil plant over intelligence ties, days before its road crossings close on 1 December, and two Libyan soldiers have died of wounds from the Ukrainian-claimed strike on Russian ships at Benghazi.

On the front, both sides are hitting energy. Ukraine reported damaging five jets at Savasleyka and drones reached refineries in Samara and a pumping station in Bashkortostan; Russia struck Kharkiv with ballistic missiles and 113 drones and hit a Kyiv shopping centre. Diplomacy is thin: Kushner says Putin is not interested in a ceasefire, the Abu Dhabi prisoner exchange has not happened, and 48 allied-funded Patriots still await Pentagon sign-off.

iran_lead.title: US disables blockade runner as Kuwait summons Iran's envoy
iran_lead.summary: US aircraft disabled the merchant ship Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on 26 November after it left Bandar Abbas, the first blockade runner hit since 7 November. Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over the drone attack that killed two Italians; Italy says the drone was Iranian-made. Iran denies launching it.
facts: 26 Nov: US aircraft disable the blockade runner Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman.
27 Nov: Kuwait summons Iran's ambassador; Italy says the Kuwait drone was Iranian-made.
28 Nov: FT: US forces repelled a drone swarm at RAF Lakenheath on 13 November; Iran suspected.
28 Nov: armed people seize a cargo ship off Balhaf, Yemen (UKMTO).
27 Nov: Mecca pact ministers pledge to intensify support for Saudi Arabia.
iran_lead.changed: The blockade was enforced with fire again: CENTCOM says aircraft hit the Pacific Archer's stern and disabled it, at least the 15th ship disabled since April by Al Jazeera's count, as Iran's navy chief vowed to break the blockade. Kuwait protested what it called continued Iranian attacks. The Financial Times reports US counter-drone systems repelled about six drones over RAF Lakenheath on 13 November, with Iran suspected. CENTCOM called Iranian claims of hitting USS Abraham Lincoln false and said that carrier returned home in October. No US strike on Iranian territory has been reported since 17 November.
iran_lead.watch: Whether Iran tries to break the blockade at sea; any US strike on Iranian soil; Italy's diplomatic response to the Kuwait deaths; who seized the cargo ship off Balhaf; OPEC+ on 29-30 November; Israel's coalition talks, as Mossad's chief backs acting alone.

brics_lead.title: Taiwan votes as Chinese military aircraft fly near the island
brics_lead.summary: Taiwan held local elections on 28 November as its defence ministry counted about 33 Chinese military aircraft sorties over two days; results were due that evening. Seoul is watching for a possible Kim Jong Un visit to China. Putin commissioned a nuclear submarine Moscow says carries Zircon hypersonic missiles.
brics_lead.changed: Taiwan accused Beijing of interfering in the vote; China rejects that. China has not announced a countermeasure to the US tariff proposal. In the CRINK lens, North Korea and Russia held their economic committee and agreed new projects, and state media said nothing about the arms pause Ukrainian intelligence claims. In Allies Cohesion, the FT reported the Lakenheath drone swarm, the IISS said Russian sabotage in Europe rose 16% in a year, and a Croatian court halted a Nord Stream suspect's extradition to Germany. Hackers breached a US Air Force cloud platform; no attacker was named.
brics_lead.watch: Taiwan's results and Beijing's reaction; any Kim visit to China; Beijing's formal response to the tariff proposal; Spain's 29 November election.

28 Nov: Seoul's spy agency watches for a possible Kim visit to China.
27 Nov: North Korea and Russia agree new economic projects.
27 Nov: Putin commissions the submarine Perm, which Moscow says carries Zircon missiles.
27 Nov: Reuters: hackers breached the US Air Force's Cloud One platform.

ukraine_lead.title: Hundreds of drones fly at Moscow; Russian strike kills seven in Nizhyn
ukraine_lead.summary: Moscow's mayor said 462 drones flew toward the capital region overnight into 28 November, suspending flights at two airports. Ukraine says it hit a Tula plant making Iskander fuel and a Rostov refinery. A Russian strike killed seven in Nizhyn. Kyiv has offered Russia a Black Sea ceasefire and awaits a reply.
facts: 28 Nov: Moscow's mayor says 462 drones flew toward the capital region.
27 Nov: Ukraine's General Staff confirms strikes on a Tula missile-fuel plant and the Novoshakhtinsk refinery.
27 Nov: a Russian strike kills seven in Nizhyn.
27 Nov: Ukraine proposes a Black Sea ceasefire.
27 Nov: Russia extends its jet fuel export ban to March 2027.
ukraine_lead.changed: Ukraine's strike campaign reached Russia's missile industry: the General Staff named the Yefremov rubber plant, which it says makes Iskander fuel, and Russia extended its jet fuel export ban to March 2027. Kyiv proposed a Black Sea ceasefire; Moscow wants oil included. A Russian convoy bound for Libya turned back after the Merkury sinking, Reuters reports. Bulgaria wants some Russian import bans lifted before backing the EU's new package. Germany approved €11.6 billion for Ukraine in 2027. A civilian exchange took place; the agreed prisoner exchange has not.
ukraine_lead.watch: Russia's reply to the Black Sea offer; the expected Russian mass strike and US approval of the 48 stalled Patriot interceptors; Estonia's 1 December border closure; whether the prisoner exchange happens; EU unanimity on the new sanctions package.
